sentences.text: Charonosaurus was a very large hadrosaur estimated to be around 10 meters in length and 5 metric tons in body mass, making it one of the largest known hadrosaurs in Asia.
This animal likely possessed a long, backward-projecting hollow crest similar to Parasaurolophus, supported by highly modified frontal bones, a feature seen in its partial skull.

The femur of Charonosaurus could reach 1.35 meters in length, longer than any other known hadrosaur of its time except Shantungosaurus giganteus, a measurement confirmed by remains of adults and juveniles found in the same area.
The genus name Charonosaurus is derived from Charon, the Greek mythological ferryman of the dead, and the Greek word for lizard.
The specific epithet jiayinensis refers to the type locality, the site of Jiayin.

Adult Charonosaurus had approximately 40 rows of teeth in the lower jaw, with only one to two teeth in use at a time, and the lower jaw teeth were very high, with dental crowns reaching up to 40 millimeters in height.

Fossils of Charonosaurus were discovered in 1975 near the city of Jiayin in the Amur region, and the species was formally described in 2000 based on a partial skeleton found in the Yuliangze Formation in Heilongjiang, China.

Charonosaurus fossils were described by Godefroit, Zan, and Jin in 2000 from the south bank of the Amur River, where they erected the species Charonosaurus jiayinensis, designating CUST J-V1251-57 as the holotype, which is a partial skull housed at the University of Science and Technology of Changchun.

The orientation of long bones suggests they were transported and deposited by a river, and hadrosaur bones from the formation were previously described by Anatoly Riabinin as Mandschurosaurus amurensis and a fragmentary hadrosaur ischium as Saurolophus krystofovici, both names previously assigned to fossils from this formation are now considered nomina dubia.

Abundant ejected teeth from carnivorous dinosaurs suggest Charonosaurus carcasses were consumed by predators and scavengers or that the animals were killed during river hunts, while dinosaur teeth found in bone beds indicate that some individuals were killed by predators or eaten by scavengers.
The sacrum of Charonosaurus consisted of nine fused vertebrae.
Charonosaurus belongs to the family Hadrosauridae and is classified in the class Ornithischia.

A 2000 cladistic analysis based on skull, teeth, and postcranial features shows Charonosaurus jiayinensis is most closely related to Parasaurolophus among Lambeosaurinae, and within the subfamily Lambeosaurinae, Charonosaurus and Parasaurolophus are closely related in the tribe Parasaurolophini, which is the parent group of Charonosaurus.

Charonosaurus is known from the Late Maastrichtian Yuliangze Formation in Heilongjiang Province, northeastern China, and lived during the Late Cretaceous, between approximately 69.9 and 66 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Charonosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Charonosaurus indicates that lambeosaurines survived until the end of the Cretaceous, a time when this group is not known from North America.

There is an ongoing debate regarding the exact phylogenetic placement of Charonosaurus, with different studies yielding conflicting results, as a 2021 study by Ramírez-Velasco et al. placed Charonosaurus closer to Tlatolophus and Blasisaurus than to Parasaurolophus.
